citations.quote: Let $F$ be either $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with conjugation equal to the identity on $\mathbb R$ and with complex conjugation as in [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]. An **inner product** on an $F$-vector space $V$ is a function $\langle\,\cdot\,,\,\cdot\,\rangle:V\times V\to F$ such that for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in F$: 1. $\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle$; 2. $\langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle}$; 3. $\langle v,v\rangle$ is real and nonnegative, and $\langle v,v\rangle=0$ if and only if $v=0$. The first two clauses imply conjugate-linearity in the second argument: $\langle u,av+bw\rangle=\overline a\langle u,v\rangle+\overline b\langle u,w\rangle$. This is the linear-first convention of [[def-sesquilinear-and-hermitian-forms-over-a-field-with-involution]]. A vector space equipped with an inner product is an **inner product space**.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with **conjugation** $z\mapsto\overline z$ the identity on $\mathbb R$ and complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$ ([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]). A **real** or **complex inner-product space** is an $\mathbb F$-vector space $V$ together with an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F$ in the sense of [[def-inner-product-space]]: for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$, $$\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle},\qquad \langle v,v\rangle\ge0,\quad \langle v,v\rangle=0\iff v=0 .$$ **Conjugate-linearity in the second argument.** Conjugate symmetry together with linearity in the first argument gives, for all $w\in V$, $$\langle w,au+bv\rangle=\overline{\langle au+bv,w\rangle}=\overline{a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle}=\overline a\,\langle w,u\rangle+\overline b\,\langle w,v\rangle .$$ **Induced length.** The **induced length**, or inner-product norm, of $v$ is $$\|v\|:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle},$$ which is exactly the published [[def-inner-product-norm]]: positive definiteness makes $\langle v,v\rangle$ a nonnegative real with a unique nonnegative square root, so that $\|v\|\ge0$, $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, and $\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2$. **The convention on this page.** Every inner-product space below is real or complex in this sense, the pairing is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second, and $\|v\|$ always denotes the induced length. In the real case conjugation is the identity and $|z|$ is the absolute value of $\mathbb R$; in the complex case they are complex conjugation and the complex modulus. All statements below are therefore written once and read in either scalar field.

Let $H$ be a real or complex inner-product space ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]), with inner product linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second, and with the induced length $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,vangle}$. The definitions below do not require completeness. When the term *Hilbert basis* is used, $H$ is additionally assumed complete ([[def-hilbert-space]]). **Orthonormal indexed family.** Let $I$ be any set. An indexed family $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ of vectors of $H$ is **orthonormal** when $$\langle e_i,e_jangle=\delta_{ij}:= egin{cases}1,&i=j,\0,&i
e j,\end{cases} \qquad	ext{for all } i,j\in I .$$Because $1
e 0$ in the scalar field, the family contains no zero vector: $\|e_i\|^2=\langle e_i,e_iangle=1$, so $\|e_i\|=1$ for every $i$ ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]); and the index map is injective, since $e_i=e_j$ with $i
e j$ would give $0=\langle e_i,e_jangle=1$. Thus an orthonormal family is the same thing as an orthonormal set together with a labelling of it, and in the sequel no choice is hidden in passing between the two descriptions. **Orthonormal set.** A subset $S\subseteq H$ is **orthonormal** when every $s\in S$ has $\|s\|=1$ and $\langle s,tangle=0$ for all distinct $s,t\in S$. For such an $S$ the family $(e_s)_{s\in S}$ with $e_s:=s$ is orthonormal in the indexed sense, and the image of an orthonormal indexed family is an orthonormal set. Orthogonal means $\langle s,tangle=0$ ([[def-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]). **Independence and unique coefficients.** Let $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ be orthonormal, let $F\subseteq I$ be finite, and let scalars $c_i$ satisfy $\sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i=0$. For each fixed $j\in F$, linearity in the first argument gives$$0=\Bigl\langle \sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i,\;e_j\Bigrangle=\sum_{i\in F}c_i\langle e_i,e_jangle=c_j ,$$ so every finite subfamily of an orthonormal family is linearly independent. In particular the coefficients in a finite expansion are unique: if $\sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i=\sum_{i\in F}d_ie_i$, then applying the computation to $c-d$ gives $c_i=d_i$ for every $i\in F$. **Closed linear span and completeness.** The **span** of an indexed family is the set of all finite linear combinations $\sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i$ with $F\subseteq I$ finite and scalars $c_i$; it is the smallest linear subspace of $H$ containing every $e_i$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]). Its closure in the induced norm is the **closed linear span** of the family, the smallest closed linear subspace of $H$ containing every $e_i$. The family is **complete**, or is a **complete orthonormal system**, when its closed linear span is all of $H$. A **Hilbert basis**, or **orthonormal basis**, of $H$ is a complete orthonormal family in $H$. **The empty family.** The span of the empty family is $\{0\}$, which is already closed, so the empty family is complete exactly when $H=\{0\}$. Thus the zero Hilbert space always has a Hilbert basis, namely the empty one. **Not a Hamel basis, and no order is assumed.** A Hilbert basis is a basis only in the sense of closed linear span: for an infinite-dimensional $H$ the vectors of $H$ are in general **not** finite linear combinations of a Hilbert basis, and the expansion of an arbitrary vector is a norm limit of finite partial sums, not a finite sum. No enumeration, ordering or countability of the index set is part of the definition; the partial sums are indexed by the finite subsets of $I$, ordered by inclusion, and that is the convention used on this page. **Coefficient notation.** For orthonormal $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ and $x\in H$ the scalars $\langle x,e_iangle$ are the **coefficients** of $x$ with respect to the family. They are well defined for every $x$, without any assumption that the family is complete.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ be an orthonormal family in a real or complex Hilbert space $H$ ([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]), and for $x\in H$ and finite $F\subseteq I$ put $$P_Fx:=\sum_{i\in F}\langle x,e_i\rangle e_i .$$ Then the following four assertions are equivalent: 1. **(completeness)** the closed linear span of $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ is $H$; 2. **(zero complement)** the only vector orthogonal to every $e_i$ is $0$; 3. **(Parseval)** $\displaystyle\sum_{i\in I}|\langle x,e_i\rangle|^2=\|x\|^2$ for every $x\in H$, the sum being the supremum of the finite subsums ([[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]]); 4. **(net convergence)** the finite-subset net $(P_Fx)_{F\in\operatorname{Fin}(I)}$ converges to $x$ for every $x\in H$. Assertion 2 is the statement $\operatorname{span}\{e_i : i\in I\}^\perp=\{0\}$ ([[def-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]).

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $M$ be a closed linear subspace of a real or complex Hilbert space $H$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]). By the orthogonal-decomposition theorem ([[thm-orthogonal-decomposition-by-a-closed-subspace]]) every $x\in H$ has a unique representation $$x=P_Mx+(x-P_Mx),\qquad P_Mx\in M,\quad x-P_Mx\in M^\perp ,$$ and the **Hilbert orthogonal projection onto $M$** is the map $$P_M:H\longrightarrow M\subseteq H,\qquad x\longmapsto P_Mx ,$$ assigning to $x$ its unique $M$-component. Its defining properties are therefore $$P_Mx\in M,\qquad x-P_Mx\in M^\perp\qquad(x\in H),$$ which characterise $P_M$ uniquely: a map with these defining properties must agree with the $M$-component of the unique decomposition of each $x$. **Agreement with the finite-dimensional projection.** If $V$ is a finite-dimensional inner-product space and $W\subseteq V$ a subspace, then [[thm-finite-dimensional-orthogonal-decomposition]] writes $V=W\oplus W^\perp$ and [[def-orthogonal-projection]] defines $P_Wv$ as the unique $W$-component of $v$; the defining properties displayed above are the same, so they define the same map on a finite-dimensional Hilbert space. **Range and kernel.** $P_Mx\in M$ for every $x$, and $P_Mm=m$ for $m\in M$ because $m=m+0$ with $0\in M^\perp$; conversely $P_Mx=0$ says exactly that $x=x-0\in M^\perp$. Hence the range of $P_M$ is $M$ and its kernel is $M^\perp$, and $P_M$ is the identity on $M$ and zero on $M^\perp$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $M$ be a closed linear subspace of a real or complex Hilbert space $H$ and let $P_M$ be the Hilbert orthogonal projection onto $M$. Then: 1. $P_M$ is linear and idempotent, $\operatorname{ran}P_M=M$ and $\ker P_M=M^\perp$; 2. $\langle P_Mx,y\rangle=\langle x,P_My\rangle$ for all $x,y\in H$, that is $P_M$ is self-adjoint; 3. $\|P_Mx\|\le\|x\|$ for every $x$, so $P_M$ is a bounded linear operator of norm at most $1$; and if $M\ne\{0\}$, then $\|P_M\|=1$.

derivations.claim: [The rotated pairs are orthonormal] By [F1] and [F2], $\langle e_{\theta},e_{\theta}\rangle=\cos^{2}\theta+\sin^{2}\theta=1$, $\langle e_{\theta}^{\perp},e_{\theta}^{\perp}\rangle=\sin^{2}\theta+\cos^{2}\theta=1$ and $\langle e_{\theta},e_{\theta}^{\perp}\rangle=-\cos\theta\sin\theta+\sin\theta\cos\theta=0$; hence $(e_{\theta},e_{\theta}^{\perp})$ is an orthonormal family of the two-dimensional space $V$, therefore an orthonormal basis of $V$. [F1, F2, algebra]

[Overlaps and the cosine identity] By [F1] and [F2], $\langle e_{\theta},\psi_{\varphi}\rangle=\cos\theta\cos\varphi+\sin\theta\sin\varphi=\cos(\theta-\varphi)$ and $\langle e_{\theta}^{\perp},\psi_{\varphi}\rangle=-\sin\theta\cos\varphi+\cos\theta\sin\varphi=\sin(\varphi-\theta)$. Then $\langle\psi_{\varphi},P_{\theta}\psi_{\varphi}\rangle=\langle\psi_{\varphi},\langle\psi_{\varphi},e_{\theta}\rangle e_{\theta}\rangle=|\langle\psi_{\varphi},e_{\theta}\rangle|^{2}=\cos^{2}(\theta-\varphi)$ because $\cos(\theta-\varphi)$ is real, and $\|P_{\theta}\psi_{\varphi}\|^{2}=|\cos(\theta-\varphi)|^{2}\|e_{\theta}\|^{2}=\cos^{2}(\theta-\varphi)$; similarly $\langle\psi_{\varphi},P_{\theta}^{\perp}\psi_{\varphi}\rangle=\sin^{2}(\theta-\varphi)$. This is (b). [F1, F2, algebra]

[The projections are orthogonal projections] For $x\in V$, $P_{\theta}x=\langle x,e_{\theta}\rangle e_{\theta}$, so $P_{\theta}(P_{\theta}x)=\langle\langle x,e_{\theta}\rangle e_{\theta},e_{\theta}\rangle e_{\theta}=\langle x,e_{\theta}\rangle\langle e_{\theta},e_{\theta}\rangle e_{\theta}=P_{\theta}x$ by [F1] and step 1.1: $P_{\theta}^{2}=P_{\theta}$. For the adjoint, $\langle P_{\theta}x,y\rangle=\langle\langle x,e_{\theta}\rangle e_{\theta},y\rangle=\langle x,e_{\theta}\rangle\langle e_{\theta},y\rangle=\langle x,\langle y,e_{\theta}\rangle e_{\theta}\rangle=\langle x,P_{\theta}y\rangle$ for all $x,y$, so $P_{\theta}^{*}=P_{\theta}$; the same computation with $e_{\theta}^{\perp}$ in place of $e_{\theta}$ gives $P_{\theta}^{\perp\,2}=P_{\theta}^{\perp}=P_{\theta}^{\perp\,*}$. By [F4] both are the orthogonal projections onto their ranges $\mathbb Ce_{\theta}$ and $\mathbb Ce_{\theta}^{\perp}$. [F1, step 1.1, F4, algebra]

[Complementarity] By step 1.1 and [F3] applied to the orthonormal basis $(e_{\theta},e_{\theta}^{\perp})$, every $x\in V$ satisfies $x=\langle x,e_{\theta}\rangle e_{\theta}+\langle x,e_{\theta}^{\perp}\rangle e_{\theta}^{\perp}=P_{\theta}x+P_{\theta}^{\perp}x$; hence $P_{\theta}+P_{\theta}^{\perp}=I$. Applying $P_{\theta}$ to the same expansion and using $P_{\theta}e_{\theta}^{\perp}=\langle e_{\theta}^{\perp},e_{\theta}\rangle e_{\theta}=0$ gives $P_{\theta}P_{\theta}^{\perp}=0$, and likewise $P_{\theta}^{\perp}P_{\theta}=0$. Since $P_{\theta}=I-P_{\theta}^{\perp}$ and $\mathbb Ce_{\theta}\cap\mathbb Ce_{\theta}^{\perp}=\{0\}$ by orthogonality of the nonzero vectors $e_{\theta},e_{\theta}^{\perp}$, the eigenspace of $P_{\theta}$ at eigenvalue $1$ is $\mathbb Ce_{\theta}$ and at eigenvalue $0$ is $\mathbb Ce_{\theta}^{\perp}$; this proves (a) and (d). [F1, F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

[Periodicity and phase invariance] Since $e_{\theta+\pi}=-e_{\theta}$ and $e_{\theta+\pi/2}=e_{\theta}^{\perp}$, the identities $P_{\theta+\pi}=P_{\theta}$ and $P_{\theta+\pi/2}=P_{\theta}^{\perp}$ follow from the definition of $P_{\theta}$ and [F1]; in particular $P_{\theta}$ is $2\pi$-periodic. For $z\ne0$ and the unit vector $\psi_{\varphi}$ one has $\|z\psi_{\varphi}\|^{2}=|z|^{2}$, and $P_{\theta}(z\psi_{\varphi})=zP_{\theta}\psi_{\varphi}$ by linearity of $x\mapsto\langle x,e_{\theta}\rangle$ in the first argument of [F1]; hence $\|P_{\theta}(z\psi_{\varphi})\|^{2}/\|z\psi_{\varphi}\|^{2}=\|P_{\theta}\psi_{\varphi}\|^{2}=\cos^{2}(\theta-\varphi)$ by step 1.2. This proves (c) and completes the proof. [F1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

citations.quote: Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]), let $d\ge1$ and work on $H=L^2(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ ([[def-hilbert-space]]). (a) For a real measurable finite-valued function $a:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ define $M_af:=af$ on $D(M_a):=\{f\in H: af\in H\}$. Then $M_a$ is a densely defined self-adjoint operator on $H$ ([[def-adjoint-of-a-densely-defined-unbounded-operator]], [[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]]). (b) Let $c>0$, $b\in\mathbb R$, and let $\mathcal F_2$ be the unitary Plancherel transform with the convention $\widehat f(\xi)=\int f(x)e^{-2\pi ix\cdot\xi}dx$ on $L^1$ ([[def-fourier-transform-on-l-one-of-rn]], [[thm-plancherel]]). Define $$H_0:=\mathcal F_2^*\,M_{c|\xi|^2+b}\,\mathcal F_2,\qquad D(H_0):=\{f\in H:|\xi|^2\mathcal F_2f\in H\}.$$ Then $H_0$ is self-adjoint, $D(H_0)$ coincides with the Sobolev space $W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ as a set (with equivalent norms, [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], [[thm-fourier-characterisation-of-integer-order-hilbert-sobolev-spaces]]), $H_0\ge b$ in the quadratic-form sense, and for every Schwartz function $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$, $H_0f=-(c/4\pi^2)\Delta f+bf$. (c) If $V:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ is measurable with $\|V\|_\infty<\infty$ and $H:=H_0+M_V$ with domain $D(H_0)$, then $H$ is self-adjoint on $D(H_0)$, is bounded below, and the assignment $t\mapsto e^{itH}$ is a strongly continuous one-parameter unitary group whose generator is $-iH$: the limit $\lim_{t\to0}\frac1t(e^{itH}\psi-\psi)$ exists exactly for $\psi\in D(H)$ and equals $iH\psi$ ([[lem-self-adjoint-operator-generates-a-strongly-continuous-unitary-group]]). (d) *Scope*: the argument uses only boundedness and measurability of $V$; it proves nothing for $V\propto-1/|x|$, $V\propto|x|^2$ or the delta interaction, does not identify $H_0$ with any measured free-particle Hamiltonian, and asserts no physical interpretation.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$ be a $\sigma$-finite measure space with $\mu(X)>0$, let $m:X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable and finite $\mu$-almost everywhere, and on the complex Hilbert space $H=L^{2}(X,\mu;\mathbb C)$ ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]], [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]], [[def-hilbert-space]]) let $$D(M_{m})=\Bigl\{f\in H:\int_{X}|m|^{2}|f|^{2}\,d\mu<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad M_{m}f=mf .$$ Then: (a) $M_{m}$ is self-adjoint on $D(M_{m})$ ([[thm-nrqm-composites-real-multipliers-and-free-bounded-potential-operators]] clause (a)). (b) The assignment $E(B):=M_{\mathbf 1_{m^{-1}(B)}}$ on Borel sets $B\subseteq\mathbb R$ is a regular projection-valued measure on the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $\mathbb R$ ([[def-projection-valued-measure]]), and for a unit vector $\psi\in H$ $$\|E(B)\psi\|^{2}=\int_{m^{-1}(B)}|\psi|^{2}\,d\mu .$$ (c) The operator identity $\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda\,dE(\lambda)=M_{m}$ holds with domain $D(M_{m})$ ([[def-unbounded-integral-against-a-pvm]]); consequently $E$ is the spectral projection-valued measure of $M_{m}$ ([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]]). (d) $E(B)=0$ if and only if $\mu(m^{-1}(B))=0$, and the spectrum $\sigma(M_{m})$ equals the essential range of $m$: $$\sigma(M_{m})=\{\,t\in\mathbb R:\mu(m^{-1}(t-\varepsilon,t+\varepsilon))>0\ \text{for every}\ \varepsilon>0\,\}.$$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $E$ be a projection valued measure on the measurable space $(X,\Sigma)$ acting on the complex Hilbert space $H$ ([[def-projection-valued-measure]]), and let $f:X\to\mathbb C$ be $\Sigma$-measurable. Put $$D(f(E)):=\Bigl\{x\in H:\int_X|f|^2\,dE_x<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad E_x(B)=\langle E(B)x,x\rangle,$$ where the scalar measures $E_x$ are those of [[lem-scalar-and-complex-measures-from-a-pvm]], and for $x\in D(f(E))$ set $$f(E)x:=\lim_{n\to\infty}\Phi_E\bigl(f\,\mathbf 1_{\{|f|\le n\}}\bigr)x,$$ For $H\ne\{0\}$, the bounded integrals $\Phi_E$ are those of [[thm-bounded-borel-pvm-integral]], and the limit is taken in the norm of $H$. For $H=\{0\}$, define $\Phi_E(g)$ to be the unique operator on $H$ for every bounded measurable $g$. Then $E_0$ is the zero measure, $D(f(E))=H$, and $f(E)0=0$. Thus this case is defined directly without applying a theorem requiring a nonzero space. **Well-definedness.** $D(f(E))$ is a linear subspace: the estimate $E_{x+y}\le2E_x+2E_y$ for scalar measures and $E_{\alpha x}=|\alpha|^2E_x$ follow from $\|E(B)(x+y)\|^2\le2\|E(B)x\|^2+2\|E(B)y\|^2$ and $\|E(B)\alpha x\|^2=|\alpha|^2\|E(B)x\|^2$. Writing $f_n:=f\mathbf 1_{\{|f|\le n\}}$ the sets $\{|f|\le n\}$ are measurable, so $f_n$ is bounded and measurable. For $m,n\ge N$, $$|f_n-f_m|^2\le |f|^2\mathbf1_{\{|f|>N\}}.$$ The integral of the right side against $E_x$ tends to zero by [[thm-dominated-convergence]], with the integrable majorant $|f|^2$ and pointwise limit zero since $f$ is finite-valued. Linearity of the bounded calculus ([[thm-pvm-integral-is-a-star-homomorphism]]) and its quadratic identity give $$\|\Phi_E(f_n)x-\Phi_E(f_m)x\|^2=\int|f_n-f_m|^2\,dE_x.$$ These clauses hold directly on the zero space as well. Hence the truncation vectors are Cauchy and converge uniquely by Hilbert-space completeness ([[def-hilbert-space]]). The limit is linear in $x$ because every truncation operator is linear and addition and scalar multiplication are norm-continuous. Countable Choice is inherited from the bounded PVM suppliers; no further choice is needed to take these specified limits. Finally, if two $\Sigma$-measurable functions $f,g$ agree outside a measurable set $N$ with $E(N)=0$, then $E_x(N)=\|E(N)x\|^2=0$ for every $x$. Thus the integrals of $|f|^2$ and $|g|^2$ agree, so their domains agree. At every truncation level their bounded truncations agree outside $N$; the quadratic identity applied to the difference gives equal truncation vectors for every $x$. Taking limits gives $f(E)x=g(E)x$ on their common domain.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $E$ be a projection valued measure on $(X,\Sigma)$ on the complex Hilbert space $H$ and let $f:X\to\mathbb C$ be $\Sigma$-measurable. Then the operator $f(E)$ of [[def-unbounded-integral-against-a-pvm]] is densely defined and closed, and it is normal, in the sense $D(f(E))=D(f(E)^*)$ and equal norms for the operator and its adjoint; in particular $D(f(E))=D(\overline f(E))$ and $\|f(E)x\|=\|\overline f(E)x\|$ for all such $x$. Moreover $$\|f(E)x\|^2=\int|f|^2\,dE_x,\qquad \langle x,f(E)x\rangle=\int\overline f\,dE_x\qquad(x\in D(f(E))),$$ and $(f(E))^*=\overline f(E)$; in particular $f(E)$ is self-adjoint whenever $f$ takes real values. Finally, if $(g_n)$ are bounded $\Sigma$-measurable functions with $|g_n|\le C|f|$ pointwise and $g_n\to f$ pointwise, then $g_n(E)x\to f(E)x$ for every $x\in D(f(E))$.

Then $M_a$ is a densely defined self-adjoint operator on $H$ ([[def-adjoint-of-a-densely-defined-unbounded-operator]], [[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]]). (b) Let $c>0$, $b\in\mathbb R$, and let $\mathcal F_2$ be the unitary Plancherel transform with the convention $\widehat f(\xi)=\int f(x)e^{-2\pi ix\cdot\xi}dx$ on $L^1$ ([[def-fourier-transform-on-l-one-of-rn]], [[thm-plancherel]]). Define $$H_0:=\mathcal F_2^*\,M_{c|\xi|^2+b}\,\mathcal F_2,\qquad D(H_0):=\{f\in H:|\xi|^2\mathcal F_2f\in H\}.$$ Then $H_0$ is self-adjoint, $D(H_0)$ coincides with the Sobolev space $W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ as a set (with equivalent norms, [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], [[thm-fourier-characterisation-of-integer-order-hilbert-sobolev-spaces]]), $H_0\ge b$ in the quadratic-form sense, and for every Schwartz function $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$, $H_0f=-(c/4\pi^2)\Delta f+bf$. (c) If $V:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ is measurable with $\|V\|_\infty<\infty$ and $H:=H_0+M_V$ with domain $D(H_0)$, then $H$ is self-adjoint on $D(H_0)$, is bounded below, and the assignment $t\mapsto e^{itH}$ is a strongly continuous one-parameter unitary group whose generator is $-iH$: the limit $\lim_{t\to0}\frac1t(e^{itH}\psi-\psi)$ exists exactly for $\psi\in D(H)$ and equals $iH\psi$ ([[lem-self-adjoint-operator-generates-a-strongly-continuous-unitary-group]]). (d) *Scope*: the argument uses only boundedness and measurability of $V$; it proves nothing for $V\propto-1/|x|$, $V\propto|x|^2$ or the delta interaction, does not identify $H_0$ with any measured free-particle Hamiltonian, and asserts no physical interpretation.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n \ge 1$ and let $f : \mathbb R^n \to \mathbb R$ be Lebesgue measurable. Then its graph $$\Gamma_f := \{(x,t) \in \mathbb R^n \times \mathbb R : t=f(x)\}$$ is Lebesgue measurable and has $(n+1)$-dimensional Lebesgue measure zero.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n \ge 1$, let $S^{n-1} \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be the unit sphere, and let $\sigma$ be the set function of [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]]. Then $\sigma$ is a finite Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$, and for every Borel measurable $f : \mathbb R^n \to [0,\infty]$, $$\int_{\mathbb R^n} f(x)\,d\lambda_n(x) = \int_0^\infty \int_{S^{n-1}} f(r\omega) r^{n-1}\,d\sigma(\omega)\,dr.$$ Moreover, $\sigma$ is the unique Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$ with this property.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice** ([[def-countable-choice]]). Every at most countable subset $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ ([[def-countable]]) is Lebesgue measurable with $$\lambda_n(E) \;=\; 0,$$ so $E$ is a $\lambda_n$-null set ([[def-measure-null-set-and-almost-everywhere]]). In particular every singleton is null, and on the real line the set $\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ of rational reals ([[lem-rat-embeds-dense]]) satisfies $\lambda_1(\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}) = 0$.

derivations.claim: [Restriction of the spectral measure] Let $m$ be one of the two displayed functions; both are real, measurable and finite-valued. By [F4] the multiplier $M_{m}$ commutes with $M_{\Pi}$, so $E(B)=M_{\mathbf 1_{m^{-1}(B)}}$ (componentwise) commutes with $M_{\Pi}$ for every Borel set $B$ and therefore maps $\mathfrak h$ into itself: for $f\in\mathfrak h$ one has $E(B)f=\mathbf 1_{m^{-1}(B)}f\in\mathfrak h$ because transversality holds pointwise. Thus $E_{\mathfrak h}(B):=E(B)|_{\mathfrak h}$ is a family of projections on $\mathfrak h$ with $E_{\mathfrak h}(B)^{2}=E_{\mathfrak h}(B)=E_{\mathfrak h}(B)^{*}$, $E_{\mathfrak h}(\varnothing)=0$, $E_{\mathfrak h}(\mathbb R)=\mathrm{id}_{\mathfrak h}$, and $\sigma$-additivity and strong convergence inherited from $E$; hence $E_{\mathfrak h}$ is a projection-valued measure on $\mathfrak h$. [F2, F4, algebra]

[No eigenvalues] Let $\lambda\in\mathbb R$ and let $f\in D(M_{m}^{\mathfrak h})$ satisfy $M_{m}^{\mathfrak h}f=\lambda f$, that is $m(k)f(k)=\lambda f(k)$ for almost every $k$. Then $f=0$ almost everywhere on $\{k:m(k)\ne\lambda\}$, so $f$ is supported in $N_{\lambda}:=\{k:m(k)=\lambda\}$ up to a null set. For $m=\hbar k_{j}$ the set $N_{\lambda}$ is null by [F5]; for $m=\hbar c|k|$ it is null by [F6]. In both cases $f=0$ almost everywhere, hence $f=0$ in $L^{2}$. This proves (c). [F5, F6, algebra]

[The restricted integral is the restricted multiplier] By [F3] applied to $E_{\mathfrak h}$ and the real function $\lambda\mapsto\lambda$ the operator $A:=\int\lambda\,dE_{\mathfrak h}(\lambda)$ is self-adjoint with domain $\{f\in\mathfrak h:\int\lambda^{2}\,dE_{\mathfrak h,f}(\lambda)<\infty\}$. For every $g\in\mathfrak h$ and Borel $B$ we have $\langle E_{\mathfrak h}(B)g,g\rangle=\int_{m^{-1}(B)}\|g(k)\|^{2}\,d^{3}k$: the scalar statements of [F2] applied to the three components of $g$ combine by sesquilinearity, and the unit case extends by scaling in $g$, so the scalar measure $E_{\mathfrak h,g}$ is the push-forward of $\|g\|^{2}\,d^{3}k$ under $k\mapsto m(k)$; hence $\int\lambda^{2}\,dE_{\mathfrak h,f}(\lambda)=\int m(k)^{2}\|f(k)\|^{2}\,d^{3}k$ by the change-of-variables formula for a push-forward measure against the Borel function $\lambda\mapsto\lambda^{2}$, the two sides agreeing on indicators of Borel sets and extending by linearity and monotone convergence. Therefore $D(A)=\{f\in\mathfrak h:\int m^{2}\|f\|^{2}\,d^{3}k<\infty\}=D(M_{m}^{\mathfrak h})$. [F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

[Identification on the domain] Let $f\in D(A)$ and put $m_{n}:=m\mathbf 1_{\{|m|\le n\}}$ for $n\ge1$; then $|m_{n}|\le|m|$ and $m_{n}\to m$ pointwise, so [F3] gives $m_{n}(E_{\mathfrak h})f\to Af$. For $g\in\mathfrak h$ the bounded operator $m_{n}(E_{\mathfrak h})$ satisfies $\langle m_{n}(E_{\mathfrak h})g,g\rangle=\int m_{n}\,dE_{\mathfrak h,g}=\int m_{n}(k)\|g(k)\|^{2}\,d^{3}k=\langle m_{n}g,g\rangle$ by the push-forward description of step 2.1; both operators are bounded and self-adjoint and their quadratic forms agree, so $m_{n}(E_{\mathfrak h})=M_{m_{n}}|_{\mathfrak h}$: the bounded functional calculus of the restricted multiplier is multiplication by $m_{n}$. The convergence $m_{n}f\to mf$ in $L^{2}(\mathbb R^{3};\mathbb C^{3})$ holds by dominated convergence, since $\|m_{n}f-mf\|^{2}\le4m^{2}\|f\|^{2}$ is integrable under $f\in D(A)$; its limit $mf$ lies in $\mathfrak h$ because transversality is preserved pointwise, with no assertion that $mf$ belongs to $D(A)$; that stronger assertion would require $m^2f\in L^2$. Hence $Af=mf=M_{m}^{\mathfrak h}f$ for every $f\in D(A)$; conversely if $f\in D(M_{m}^{\mathfrak h})$ then $\int m^{2}\|f\|^{2}=\|mf\|^{2}<\infty$, so $f\in D(A)$. Therefore $A=M_{m}^{\mathfrak h}$ with the displayed domain, and (a) and (b) follow. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

[Positive variance] Let $f\in\mathfrak h$ be a unit vector in $D(M_{m}^{\mathfrak h})$ and put $\mu:=\langle M_{m}^{\mathfrak h}f,f\rangle$, a real number because $M_{m}^{\mathfrak h}$ is self-adjoint. Then $$\|M_{m}^{\mathfrak h}f\|^{2}-\langle M_{m}^{\mathfrak h}f,f\rangle^{2}=\|(M_{m}^{\mathfrak h}-\mu I)f\|^{2}\ge0,$$ and equality holds exactly when $(M_{m}^{\mathfrak h}-\mu I)f=0$, that is when $f$ is an eigenvector of $M_{m}^{\mathfrak h}$ with eigenvalue $\mu$. By step 1.2 no nonzero eigenvector exists, so the left-hand side is strictly positive. This proves (d) and completes the proof. [step 1.2, algebra] ∎

boundaries.evidence: Step 1.2 covers the empty level set for lambda < 0 in the energy case via Fact F6, where {hbar c |k| = lambda} is empty
Step 1.2 covers lambda = 0: the hyperplane {k_j = 0} is null by F5 and {k = 0} is a null singleton in the energy case by F6
Step 4.1 quantifies over unit f in D(M_m^h) and proves the variance identity and its strict positivity
Step 1.2 proves that no eigenvalue exists for either multiplier; step 4.1 uses this to exclude the equality case of the variance

Statement(a)-(b) establish self-adjoint restricted multipliers and their PVM; (c)-(d) exclude eigenvectors and prove positive variance. No reverse inference from a measurement law to transversality is asserted. The reverse iff boundary is therefore not a separate obligation.

citations.quote: Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space with inner product linear in the first argument ([[def-hilbert-space]], [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). Let $H^{\otimes 0}:=\mathbb C$, $H^{\otimes 1}:=H$ and $H^{\otimes(n+1)}:=H^{\otimes n}\widehat\otimes H$ be the completed tensor powers with elementary tensors $u_1\otimes\cdots\otimes u_n$ ([[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]]); for $n\ge 1$ let $P_+^{(n)}\in\mathcal B(H^{\otimes n})$ be the symmetric projection of [[lem-nrqm-composites-permutation-sector-projections]] and set $P_+^{(0)}:=\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb C}$. Write $\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$ for its range and define $$F(H):=\Bigl\{\psi=(\psi_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}:\ \psi_n\in\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}\ \text{for all }n,\ \sum_{n\in\mathbb N}\|\psi_n\|^2<\infty\Bigr\}.$$ Then: (a) for $\psi,\varphi\in F(H)$ the scalar series $\sum_{n\in\mathbb N}\langle\psi_n,\varphi_n\rangle$ converges absolutely and defines a sesquilinear form, linear in the first argument, with respect to which $F(H)$ is a complex vector space with inner product $\langle\psi,\varphi\rangle:=\sum_{n\in\mathbb N}\langle\psi_n,\varphi_n\rangle$ ([[cor-cauchy-schwarz-inequality-for-l-two]], [[def-series-and-absolute-convergence-in-a-normed-space]]); (b) $(F(H),\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle)$ is a Hilbert space, i.e. the induced norm is complete ([[def-hilbert-space]]); (c) the vacuum vector $\Omega:=(1,0,0,\dots)$ satisfies $\|\Omega\|=1$, and the finite-particle space $F_0:=\{\psi\in F(H):\psi_n=0\ \text{for all but finitely many }n\}$ is a dense linear subspace of $F(H)$ ([[def-dense-top]]); (d) for every $n$ the map $\iota_n:\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}\to F(H)$, $\iota_n(u):=(0,\dots,0,u,0,\dots)$ (entry in coordinate $n$) is a linear isometry of $\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$ onto the closed subspace of vectors supported in coordinate $n$; (e) if $H$ admits a countable complete orthonormal family $(e_i)_{i\in I}$, $I$ at most countable ([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]), then $F(H)$ is separable ([[def-separable-space]]); (f) *direct sums of self-adjoint operators*: if for every $n\ge 1$ a self-adjoint operator $T_n$ on the Hilbert space $\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$ with domain $D(T_n)\subseteq\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$ is given ([[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]], [[def-unbounded-linear-operator-domain-and-graph]]), and $$D(T):=\Bigl\{\psi\in F(H):\ \psi_n\in D(T_n)\ \text{for all }n,\ \sum_{n\in\mathbb N}\|T_n\psi_n\|^2<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad (T\psi)_n:=T_n\psi_n,$$ then $T$ is self-adjoint and $D(T)$ is dense; if in addition every $T_n$ is bounded with $\sup_{n}\|T_n\|<\infty$, then $T$ is bounded with $\|T\|=\sup_n\|T_n\|$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). No physical interpretation of $F(H)$, of the tensor powers or of the direct-sum operators is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space, $n\ge1$, and $H^{\otimes n}$ the $n$-fold completed tensor power ($H^{\otimes1}:=H$, $H^{\otimes(k+1)}:=H^{\otimes k}\widehat\otimes H$ as in [[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]]). For $v_1,\dots,v_n\in H$ write $v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n\in H^{\otimes n}$ for the iterated elementary tensor. (a) For every $\pi$ in the symmetric group $S_n$ ([[def-finite-symmetric-group-and-permutation-notation]]) there is a unique unitary $U_\pi\in\mathcal B(H^{\otimes n})$ with $$U_\pi(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)=v_{\pi^{-1}(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{\pi^{-1}(n)},$$ and $U_\pi U_\sigma=U_{\pi\sigma}$, $U_{\pi}^*=U_{\pi^{-1}}$. (b) The operators $$P_+:=\frac1{n!}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}U_\pi,\qquad P_-:=\frac1{n!}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)U_\pi$$ (with $\operatorname{sgn}$ the sign homomorphism, [[thm-sign-is-a-homomorphism]]) are orthogonal projections. (c) $U_\pi P_+=P_+U_\pi=P_+$ and $U_\pi P_-=P_-U_\pi=\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)P_-$ for every $\pi$; consequently the range of $P_+$ is the subspace of vectors fixed by every $U_\pi$, and the range of $P_-$ is the subspace of vectors transforming by $\operatorname{sgn}$. (d) If $v_1,\dots,v_n$ are not pairwise distinct in the sense that $v_i=v_j$ for some $i\ne j$, then $P_-(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)=0$; in particular, for $n\ge2$, $P_-(u\otimes u\otimes w_3\otimes\cdots\otimes w_n)=0$ for all $u,w_k\in H$. Selecting the symmetric or antisymmetric sector for a particle species is a physical postulate, not a theorem of this construction; no spin-statistics statement is proved here.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H,K$ be complex Hilbert spaces with the pairing linear in the first argument ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]], [[def-hilbert-space]]). Write $H\odot K$ for the complex vector space of [[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]] applied to $R=\mathbb C$ and the $\mathbb C$-modules $H,K$: its underlying abelian group is the quotient $F/H_0$ of that definition, the class of $e_{(u,v)}$ is written $u\otimes v$, every element of $H\odot K$ is a finite sum of elementary tensors $u\otimes v$, and the defining relations make $(u,v)\mapsto u\otimes v$ $\mathbb C$-bilinear. Define, for finite sums, $$\Bigl\langle\sum_i u_i\otimes v_i,\ \sum_j u'_j\otimes v'_j\Bigr\rangle:=\sum_{i,j}\langle u_i,u'_j\rangle_H\,\langle v_i,v'_j\rangle_K .$$ Then: (a) *well-definedness and sesquilinearity*: the displayed value is independent of the representatives of its two arguments and defines a Hermitian sesquilinear form on $H\odot K$, linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second; (b) *positive definiteness and orthonormal coordinates*: $\langle z,z\rangle\ge0$ for every $z\in H\odot K$, with $\langle z,z\rangle=0$ exactly for $z=0$; more precisely, if $U_0\subseteq H$ and $V_0\subseteq K$ are finite-dimensional subspaces with orthonormal bases $e_1,\dots,e_p$ and $f_1,\dots,f_q$, then every $z$ in the span of the elementary tensors from $U_0\times V_0$ has a unique expansion $z=\sum_{a,b}c_{ab}\,e_a\otimes f_b$ and $\langle z,z\rangle=\sum_{a,b}|c_{ab}|^2$; in particular the assignment is an inner product on $H\odot K$; (c) *completion*: the norm completion $(\widehat{H\odot K},\kappa)$ of $H\odot K$ ([[def-completion-of-a-normed-space]]) exists and, with the unique inner product extending the given one, is a complex Hilbert space; $\kappa$ is a linear isometry with dense image, $\|\kappa(u\otimes v)\|=\|u\|\,\|v\|$, and any two completions of $H\odot K$ are identified by a unique surjective linear isometry fixing $H\odot K$ pointwise; (d) *product bases*: if $(e_a)_{a\in A}$ and $(f_b)_{b\in B}$ are orthonormal families in $H$ and $K$ whose closed linear spans are $H$ and $K$, then $(\kappa(e_a\otimes f_b))_{(a,b)\in A\times B}$ is an orthonormal family in $\widehat{H\odot K}$ whose closed linear span is $\widehat{H\odot K}$; if $A$ and $B$ are countable then $\widehat{H\odot K}$ is separable. The notation $H\widehat{\otimes}K:=\widehat{H\odot K}$ is used in the rest of this pair. No assertion is made about unbounded operators or algebraic sums of non-completed tensor products.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space with completed tensor powers $H^{\otimes n}$, symmetric projections $P_+^{(n)}$ and Fock space $F(H)$ as in [[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-hilbert-direct-sum-construction]]. Define the number operator by $$D(N):=\Bigl\{\psi\in F(H):\ \sum_{n\in\mathbb N}n^2\|\psi_n\|^2<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad (N\psi)_n:=n\psi_n .$$ Then: (a) $N$ is a densely defined self-adjoint operator on $F(H)$ with the displayed domain; $N\ge0$ in the sense that $\langle N\psi,\psi\rangle\ge0$ for $\psi\in D(N)$, $N\Omega=0$, and $F_0$ is a core for $N$ ([[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]]); (b) for every $n$, every nonzero $u\in\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$ satisfies $N\iota_n(u)=n\,\iota_n(u)$, and for $H\ne\{0\}$ the spectrum of $N$ is $\sigma(N)=\mathbb N$; (c) for $f\in H$ and $\psi\in F_0$ the core operators of [[lem-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-creation-contraction-bounds]] satisfy $$N S_+(f)\psi-S_+(f)N\psi=S_+(f)\psi,\qquad N S_-(f)\psi-S_-(f)N\psi=-S_-(f)\psi ;$$ (d) $D(N)\subseteq D_1:=\{\psi:\sum_n(n+1)\|\psi_n\|^2<\infty\}$, and for every $\psi\in D(N)$, $$\|N\psi\|^2=\sum_{n\in\mathbb N}n^2\|\psi_n\|^2,\qquad \langle N\psi,\psi\rangle=\sum_{n\in\mathbb N}n\|\psi_n\|^2 .$$ No physical interpretation of $N$, and no assertion about particle number measurement, is made.

Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) with completed tensor powers $H^{\otimes n}$ and symmetric projections $P_+^{(n)}$ as in [[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-hilbert-direct-sum-construction]], so that $$F(H)=\Bigl\{\psi=(\psi_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}:\ \psi_n\in\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)},\ \sum_n\|\psi_n\|^2<\infty\Bigr\}$$ is a Hilbert space. For $n\in\mathbb N$ define $$\Pi_n:F(H)	o F(H),\qquad \Pi_n\psi:=(0,\dots,0,\psi_n,0,\dots)$$ (the entry $\psi_n$ in coordinate $n$ and $0$ in all other coordinates). Then: (a) each $\Pi_n$ is a bounded linear operator with $\|\Pi_n\psi\|=\|\psi_n\|$ and $\|\Pi_n\|\le1$; it satisfies $\Pi_n^2=\Pi_n$, $\Pi_n^*=\Pi_n$ ([[def-hilbert-space-adjoint]]), and $\Pi_n$ is the Hilbert orthogonal projection of $F(H)$ onto the closed subspace $\iota_n(\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)})$ of vectors supported in coordinate $n$ ([[def-hilbert-orthogonal-projection]]); (b) $\Pi_n\Pi_m=0$ for $n
e m$, so the ranges are pairwise orthogonal and $\|\Pi_n\|=1$ whenever $\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}
e\{0\}$ (which holds for every $n$ when $H
e\{0\}$); (c) for every $\psi\in F(H)$ the series $\sum_{n}\Pi_n\psi$ converges in norm to $\psi$, the expansion is orthogonal, $$\psi=\sum_{n\in\mathbb N}\Pi_n\psi,\qquad \|\psi\|^2=\sum_{n\in\mathbb N}\|\Pi_n\psi\|^2,$$ and the partial sums $\sum_{n\le N}\Pi_n$ converge to the identity in the strong operator topology, i.e. $ igl\|\psi-\sum_{n\le N}\Pi_n\psi igr\|	o0$ for every $\psi\in F(H)$ ([[def-dense-top]], [[def-bounded-linear-operator]]); (d) $\Pi_n=0$ as an operator if and only if $\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}=\{0\}$; for $H
e\{0\}$ no $\Pi_n$ vanishes. No physical interpretation of the Fock space or of its sectors is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) with completed tensor powers $H^{\otimes n}$, symmetric projections $P_+^{(n)}$, contraction maps $\Psi_f^{(n)}$, Fock space $F(H)$ and core operators $S_\pm(f)$ on the finite-particle space $F_0$ as in [[lem-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-creation-contraction-bounds]]. For $f\in H$ define $$D(A_+(f)):=\Bigl\{\psi\in F(H):\ \sum_{n\in\mathbb N}(n+1)\bigl\|P_+^{(n+1)}(f\otimes\psi_n)\bigr\|^2<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad (A_+(f)\psi)_n:=\sqrt n\,P_+^{(n)}(f\otimes\psi_{n-1})\ (n\ge1),\ (A_+(f)\psi)_0:=0,$$ $$D(A_-(f)):=\Bigl\{\psi\in F(H):\ \sum_{n\in\mathbb N}(n+1)\bigl\|\Psi_f^{(n)}(\psi_{n+1})\bigr\|^2<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad (A_-(f)\psi)_n:=\sqrt{n+1}\,\Psi_f^{(n)}(\psi_{n+1}).$$ Put $D_1:=\{\psi\in F(H):\sum_n(n+1)\|\psi_n\|^2<\infty\}$. Then: (a) $A_+(f)$ and $A_-(f)$ are well-defined linear operators on $F(H)$ with the displayed domains, and they are the closure and the adjoint of the core operator: $$A_+(f)=\overline{S_+(f)}=S_-(f)^*,\qquad A_-(f)=S_+(f)^*=\overline{S_-(f)}$$ ([[def-adjoint-of-a-densely-defined-unbounded-operator]], [[def-densely-defined-closed-and-closable-operator]], [[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]]); (b) both $A_\pm(f)$ are closed, densely defined and satisfy $A_+(f)^*=A_-(f)$, $A_-(f)^*=A_+(f)$; in particular $F_0\subseteq D_1\subseteq D(A_\pm(f))$; (c) for every $\psi\in D_1$, $\|A_+(f)\psi\|\le\|f\|\,\|\psi\|_1$ and $\|A_-(f)\psi\|\le\|f\|\,\|\psi\|_1$, where $\|\psi\|_1^2=\sum_n(n+1)\|\psi_n\|^2$; (d) for every $g\in H$ and $\psi\in D_1$ the identity $$\|A_+(g)\psi\|^2=\|A_-(g)\psi\|^2+\|g\|^2\|\psi\|^2$$ holds. No boundedness of $A_\pm(f)$ on $F(H)$, no self-adjointness of $A_\pm(f)$, and no physical interpretation is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space with inner product linear in the first argument ([[def-hilbert-space]], [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]), with completed tensor powers $H^{\otimes n}$, symmetric projections $P_+^{(n)}$, Fock space $F(H)$ and finite-particle space $F_0$ as in [[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-hilbert-direct-sum-construction]] and [[lem-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-fock-sector-projections]]. (a) *Contraction map.* For every $f\in H$ and $n\ge0$ there is a unique bounded linear map $\Psi_f^{(n)}:H^{\otimes(n+1)}\to H^{\otimes n}$ with $$\langle\varphi,\Psi_f^{(n)}\chi\rangle=\langle f\otimes\varphi,\chi\rangle \qquad(\varphi\in H^{\otimes n},\ \chi\in H^{\otimes(n+1)})$$ ([[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]]); it satisfies $\|\Psi_f^{(n)}\|\le\|f\|$, $\Psi_f^{(n)}(u_1\otimes\cdots\otimes u_{n+1})=\langle u_1,f\rangle\,u_2\otimes\cdots\otimes u_{n+1}$ on elementary tensors, $\Psi_f^{(n)}(\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n+1)})\subseteq\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$, and the map $f\mapsto\Psi_f^{(n)}$ is conjugate-linear. (b) *Creation and annihilation on the core.* Define, for $f\in H$ and $\psi\in F_0$, $$(S_+(f)\psi)_n:=\sqrt n\,P_+^{(n)}(f\otimes\psi_{n-1})\ (n\ge1),\quad (S_+(f)\psi)_0:=0,$$ $$(S_-(f)\psi)_n:=\sqrt{n+1}\,\Psi_f^{(n)}(\psi_{n+1})\ (n\ge0).$$ Then $S_+(f)\psi,S_-(f)\psi\in F_0$; $S_+(f)$ is linear in $f$ and $S_-(f)$ is conjugate-linear in $f$; and with $\|\psi\|_1^2:=\sum_{n}\bigl(n+1\bigr)\|\psi_n\|^2<\infty$ for $\psi\in F_0$, $$\|S_+(f)\psi\|\le\|f\|\,\|\psi\|_1,\qquad \|S_-(f)\psi\|\le\|f\|\,\|\psi\|_1.$$ (c) *Adjoint relation.* $\langle S_+(f)\varphi,\psi\rangle=\langle\varphi,S_-(f)\psi\rangle$ for all $f\in H$ and $\varphi,\psi\in F_0$ ([[def-operator-norm]], [[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). (d) *Canonical commutation relation.* For all $f,g\in H$ and $\psi\in F_0$, $$S_-(f)S_+(g)\psi-S_+(g)S_-(f)\psi=\langle g,f\rangle\,\psi,$$ and consequently $$\|S_+(g)\psi\|^2=\|S_-(g)\psi\|^2+\|g\|^2\|\psi\|^2.$$ Neither $S_+(f)$ nor $S_-(f)$ is asserted to be bounded on $F(H)$, and no physical interpretation (particle creation, radiation or measurement) is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$\mathbb H:=\mathbb C$ with its standard inner product (linear in the first
argument), let $F(\mathbb C)$ be its Fock space as in
[[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-hilbert-direct-sum-construction]], let
$e_n\in F(\mathbb C)$ be the unit vector supported in coordinate $n$ (so
$(e_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ is a complete orthonormal family of $F(\mathbb C)$),
let $N$ be the number operator and let $A_\pm(1)$ be the maximal creation and
annihilation operators of
[[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-closed-adjoint-sector-domains]] for the vector
$1\in\mathbb C$. Then:

(a) *oscillator coefficients*: for every $n\in\mathbb N$,
$$A_+(1)e_n=\sqrt{n+1}\,e_{n+1},\qquad A_-(1)e_n=\sqrt n\,e_{n-1}\ (n\ge1),\qquad A_-(1)e_0=0;$$

(b) *coherent vectors*: for every $z\in\mathbb C$ the series
$$\psi_z:=e^{-|z|^2/2}\sum_{n\in\mathbb N}\frac{z^n}{\sqrt{n!}}\,e_n$$
converges absolutely in $F(\mathbb C)$
([[def-complex-exponential]], [[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]]),
$\|\psi_z\|=1$, $\psi_z\in D(A_-(1))$ with
$$A_-(1)\psi_z=z\,\psi_z,$$
and for all $z,w\in\mathbb C$,
$$\langle\psi_z,\psi_w\rangle=e^{-(|z|^2+|w|^2)/2+z\overline w};$$

(c) *number law*: for every $n\in\mathbb N$,
$$\bigl|\langle e_n,\psi_z\rangle\bigr|^2=e^{-|z|^2}\frac{|z|^{2n}}{n!},$$
and $\sum_{n\in\mathbb N}|\langle e_n,\psi_z\rangle|^2=1$.

The numbers in (c) are squared moduli of overlaps of unit vectors; identifying
them with outcome probabilities of a number measurement requires a separately
adopted measurement postulate, and no such physical claim is made here.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice, the Axiom of Dependent Choice and the Axiom of Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Fix a parameter $\alpha>0$, define the transverse subspace $$\mathfrak h:=\Bigl\{f\in L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^3):\ k\cdot f(k)=0\ \text{for a.e. }k\Bigr\}$$ with the $L^2$ inner product, define the bounded multiplier-valued function $\Pi(k):=\mathrm{id}-|k|^{-2}kk^{\mathsf T}$ for $k\ne0$ and $\Pi(0):=0$, and let $M_\Pi$ be multiplication by $\Pi$ on $L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^3)$ ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]], [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]). Write $\varepsilon(k):=\alpha|k|$ and let $M_\varepsilon$ be multiplication by $\varepsilon$, with $\varepsilon_{\mathfrak h}:=M_\varepsilon|_{\mathfrak h}$. Let $F(\mathfrak h)$ be the Fock space of [[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-hilbert-direct-sum-construction]] with sectors $\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$, and for $n\ge1$ define $$T_n\psi:=\varepsilon_n\psi,\quad \varepsilon_n(k_1,\dots,k_n):=\sum_{i=1}^n\alpha|k_i|,\qquad D(T_n):=\{\psi\in\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}:\varepsilon_n\psi\in\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}\},$$ and $T_0:=0$ on $\mathbb C$. Finally put $$H_f:=\bigoplus_{n\ge0}T_n,\qquad D(H_f):=\Bigl\{\psi\in F(\mathfrak h):\ \sum_n\|T_n\psi_n\|^2<\infty\Bigr\}.$$ Then: (a) $\mathfrak h=\operatorname{ran}M_\Pi$ is a closed separable subspace of $L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^3)$, invariant under $M_\varepsilon$, and $\varepsilon_{\mathfrak h}$ is a positive self-adjoint operator on $\mathfrak h$ with $D(\varepsilon_{\mathfrak h})=\{f\in\mathfrak h:\varepsilon f\in\mathfrak h\}$ ([[thm-nrqm-composites-real-multipliers-and-free-bounded-potential-operators]], [[def-hilbert-orthogonal-projection]]); (b) each $T_n$ is a positive self-adjoint operator on the Hilbert space $\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$ with the displayed domain ([[def-hilbert-space]], [[lem-nrqm-composites-euclidean-l2-product-unitary]], [[lem-nrqm-composites-permutation-sector-projections]]); (c) $H_f$ is self-adjoint and positive with domain $D(H_f)$; it commutes with every sector projection $\Pi_n$ (i.e. $T_n$ maps its sector into itself); (d) for every $\beta>0$ the bounded operator $e^{-\beta H_f}$ ([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]], [[def-projection-valued-measure]]) is not compact and in particular not trace class ([[def-compact-linear-operator]], [[def-trace-class-operator]]); more precisely its restriction to the one-particle sector equals the multiplication operator $M_{e^{-\beta\varepsilon}}$ on $\mathfrak h$, which is not compact, and the restriction of a compact operator to a closed invariant subspace is compact. The identification of $\mathfrak h$, $\varepsilon$ and $H_f$ with physical transverse photons in a chosen frame is a separate model assumption and is not asserted here; no thermal interpretation of $e^{-\beta H_f}$ is claimed either.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space, $n\ge1$, and $H^{\otimes n}$ the $n$-fold completed tensor power ($H^{\otimes1}:=H$, $H^{\otimes(k+1)}:=H^{\otimes k}\widehat\otimes H$ as in [[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]]). For $v_1,\dots,v_n\in H$ write $v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n\in H^{\otimes n}$ for the iterated elementary tensor. (a) For every $\pi$ in the symmetric group $S_n$ ([[def-finite-symmetric-group-and-permutation-notation]]) there is a unique unitary $U_\pi\in\mathcal B(H^{\otimes n})$ with $$U_\pi(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)=v_{\pi^{-1}(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{\pi^{-1}(n)},$$ and $U_\pi U_\sigma=U_{\pi\sigma}$, $U_{\pi}^*=U_{\pi^{-1}}$. (b) The operators $$P_+:=\frac1{n!}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}U_\pi,\qquad P_-:=\frac1{n!}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)U_\pi$$ (with $\operatorname{sgn}$ the sign homomorphism, [[thm-sign-is-a-homomorphism]]) are orthogonal projections. (c) $U_\pi P_+=P_+U_\pi=P_+$ and $U_\pi P_-=P_-U_\pi=\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)P_-$ for every $\pi$; consequently the range of $P_+$ is the subspace of vectors fixed by every $U_\pi$, and the range of $P_-$ is the subspace of vectors transforming by $\operatorname{sgn}$. (d) If $v_1,\dots,v_n$ are not pairwise distinct in the sense that $v_i=v_j$ for some $i\ne j$, then $P_-(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)=0$; in particular, for $n\ge2$, $P_-(u\otimes u\otimes w_3\otimes\cdots\otimes w_n)=0$ for all $u,w_k\in H$. Selecting the symmetric or antisymmetric sector for a particle species is a physical postulate, not a theorem of this construction; no spin-statistics statement is proved here.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H,K$ be complex Hilbert spaces with the pairing linear in the first argument ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]], [[def-hilbert-space]]). Write $H\odot K$ for the complex vector space of [[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]] applied to $R=\mathbb C$ and the $\mathbb C$-modules $H,K$: its underlying abelian group is the quotient $F/H_0$ of that definition, the class of $e_{(u,v)}$ is written $u\otimes v$, every element of $H\odot K$ is a finite sum of elementary tensors $u\otimes v$, and the defining relations make $(u,v)\mapsto u\otimes v$ $\mathbb C$-bilinear. Define, for finite sums, $$\Bigl\langle\sum_i u_i\otimes v_i,\ \sum_j u'_j\otimes v'_j\Bigr\rangle:=\sum_{i,j}\langle u_i,u'_j\rangle_H\,\langle v_i,v'_j\rangle_K .$$ Then: (a) *well-definedness and sesquilinearity*: the displayed value is independent of the representatives of its two arguments and defines a Hermitian sesquilinear form on $H\odot K$, linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second; (b) *positive definiteness and orthonormal coordinates*: $\langle z,z\rangle\ge0$ for every $z\in H\odot K$, with $\langle z,z\rangle=0$ exactly for $z=0$; more precisely, if $U_0\subseteq H$ and $V_0\subseteq K$ are finite-dimensional subspaces with orthonormal bases $e_1,\dots,e_p$ and $f_1,\dots,f_q$, then every $z$ in the span of the elementary tensors from $U_0\times V_0$ has a unique expansion $z=\sum_{a,b}c_{ab}\,e_a\otimes f_b$ and $\langle z,z\rangle=\sum_{a,b}|c_{ab}|^2$; in particular the assignment is an inner product on $H\odot K$; (c) *completion*: the norm completion $(\widehat{H\odot K},\kappa)$ of $H\odot K$ ([[def-completion-of-a-normed-space]]) exists and, with the unique inner product extending the given one, is a complex Hilbert space; $\kappa$ is a linear isometry with dense image, $\|\kappa(u\otimes v)\|=\|u\|\,\|v\|$, and any two completions of $H\odot K$ are identified by a unique surjective linear isometry fixing $H\odot K$ pointwise; (d) *product bases*: if $(e_a)_{a\in A}$ and $(f_b)_{b\in B}$ are orthonormal families in $H$ and $K$ whose closed linear spans are $H$ and $K$, then $(\kappa(e_a\otimes f_b))_{(a,b)\in A\times B}$ is an orthonormal family in $\widehat{H\odot K}$ whose closed linear span is $\widehat{H\odot K}$; if $A$ and $B$ are countable then $\widehat{H\odot K}$ is separable. The notation $H\widehat{\otimes}K:=\widehat{H\odot K}$ is used in the rest of this pair. No assertion is made about unbounded operators or algebraic sums of non-completed tensor products.

derivations.claim: [The powers of $\varphi$ are orthonormal sector vectors] For $n\ge0$ put $\Phi_n:=\varphi^{\otimes n}$, with $\Phi_0:=1$. By [F2] with $u=\varphi$ and $\|\varphi\|=1$ one has $\|\Phi_n\|=1$ for every $n$, $P_+^{(n)}\Phi_n=\Phi_n$, and $\langle\Phi_n,\Phi_n\rangle=\prod_{i=1}^{n}\langle\varphi,\varphi\rangle=1$; for $m\ne n$ the pairing $\langle\Phi_m,\Phi_n\rangle$ vanishes because $\Phi_m$ is supported in the direct-sum coordinate $m$ and $\Phi_n$ in coordinate $n$, and the inner product of $F(H)$ is the sum of the coordinate pairings by [F1]. Hence $(\Phi_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ is an orthonormal family with $\Phi_n\in\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$ for every $n$. [F1, F2, algebra]

[The isometry] Define $U_\varphi$ on the finite linear span of $(e_n)$ by $U_\varphi e_n=\Phi_n$ and extend by linearity; by step 1.1, $\|U_\varphi\psi\|^{2}=\sum_n|\psi_n|^{2}=\|\psi\|^{2}$ for every finite combination, so $U_\varphi$ is isometric on the dense finite-particle subspace $F_0(\mathbb C)$ of [[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-hilbert-direct-sum-construction]] clause (c) and extends uniquely to an isometry $U_\varphi:F(\mathbb C)\to F(H)$ with the same norm identity for all $\psi\in F(\mathbb C)$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]], [[thm-parseval-equivalences-for-a-complete-orthonormal-family]]). Its range is the closed linear span of $(\Phi_n)$, since an isometry maps the closed span of an orthonormal family onto the closed span of its image and the image family is orthonormal; this proves (a). [F1, F2, algebra]

[Ladder transfer on the exact domains] Write $\psi=\sum_n\psi_ne_n$. By [F4] and [F5], $\psi\in D(A_+(1))$ exactly when $\sum_n(n+1)|\psi_n|^2<\infty$, while $\psi\in D(A_-(1))$ exactly when $\sum_n(n+1)|\psi_{n+1}|^2=\sum_{m\ge1}m|\psi_m|^2<\infty$. For the unit mode $\varphi$, [F2] gives $P_+^{(n+1)}(\varphi\otimes\psi_n\Phi_n)=\psi_n\Phi_{n+1}$ and [F4] gives $\Psi_\varphi^{(n)}(\psi_{n+1}\Phi_{n+1})=\psi_{n+1}\Phi_n$. Therefore the two exact domain sums for $U_\varphi\psi$ equal the respective scalar sums, without any extra weighted output assumption. On these domains, $(A_+(\varphi)U_\varphi\psi)_n=\sqrt n\psi_{n-1}\Phi_n=(U_\varphi A_+(1)\psi)_n$ for $n\ge1$, with zero vacuum coordinate, and $(A_-(\varphi)U_\varphi\psi)_n=\sqrt{n+1}\psi_{n+1}\Phi_n=(U_\varphi A_-(1)\psi)_n$. This proves (c), including its coherent-vector specialization by [F5]. [F2, F4, F5, step 1.1, algebra]

[Energy expectation] Assume now $H=\mathfrak h$ and $\varphi$ unit with $\varepsilon\varphi\in\mathfrak h$; write $\bar\varepsilon:=\langle\varepsilon\varphi,\varphi\rangle$. For fixed $n$, $\Phi_n=\varphi^{\otimes n}\in\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$ and, by [F6], $T_n\Phi_n=\varepsilon_n\Phi_n$; using the Euclidean identification and the symmetry of $\varepsilon_n$ under the permutation action, the iterated $L^{2}$ integral gives $$\langle T_n\Phi_n,\Phi_n\rangle=\int_{(\mathbb R^{3})^{n}}\Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\varepsilon(k_i)\Bigr)\prod_{i=1}^{n}\|\varphi(k_i)\|_{\mathbb C^{3}}^{2}\,d^{3}k_1\cdots d^{3}k_n=n\,\bar\varepsilon\,\|\varphi\|^{2(n-1)}=n\,\bar\varepsilon,$$ each of the $n$ summands contributing the same product $\bar\varepsilon\|\varphi\|^{2(n-1)}$ by Tonelli's theorem, the product measure being $\sigma$-finite and the integrand nonnegative; this is finite because $\varepsilon\varphi\in L^{2}$ and $\varphi\in L^{2}$ give $\int\varepsilon\|\varphi\|^{2}\le\|\varepsilon\varphi\|\,\|\varphi\|<\infty$. The actual domain is also justified: by the triangle inequality on the product space, $\|T_n\Phi_n\|\le n\|\varepsilon\varphi\|$, since each factor multiplier has that norm and all other factors have norm one. Hence $\sum_n|\psi_n|^2\|T_n\Phi_n\|^2\le\|\varepsilon\varphi\|^2\sum_n n^2|\psi_n|^2<\infty$, so $U_\varphi\psi\in D(H_f)$ and its finite-sector truncations converge in the graph norm: the squared graph-tail norms are the tails of these two convergent nonnegative series. Therefore for a finite combination the sector-diagonal form of $H_f$ (clause (c) of [F6]) gives $\langle H_fU_\varphi\psi,U_\varphi\psi\rangle=\sum_n|\psi_n|^{2}\,n\bar\varepsilon$; the general case $\sum_nn^{2}|\psi_n|^{2}<\infty$ follows by approximation with truncations in the graph norm of $H_f$ (both sides are continuous under this approximation, the left because $H_f$ is closed and self-adjoint, the right by dominated convergence). This proves the first two displays of (d). [F3, F6, step 1.1, algebra]

[Sector and number transfer] For $\psi=\sum_m\psi_me_m$ in the dense span and fixed $n$, $\Pi_nU_\varphi\psi=\psi_n\Phi_n=U_\varphi(\psi_ne_n)=U_\varphi\Pi_n'\psi$; since both sides are bounded in $\psi$ and the span is dense, the identity extends to all $\psi\in F(\mathbb C)$, and the norm identity is step 2.1. For $\psi\in F(\mathbb C)$ the coefficient vector of $U_\varphi\psi$ is again $(\psi_n)$, so $\sum_nn^{2}\|(U_\varphi\psi)_n\|^{2}=\sum_nn^{2}|\psi_n|^{2}$: $U_\varphi\psi\in D(N)$ exactly when $\psi\in D(N')$, and then $(NU_\varphi\psi)_n=n\psi_n\Phi_n=(U_\varphi N'\psi)_n$ for every $n$ by [F3]. This proves (b). [F1, F3, step 2.1, algebra]

[Spectral second moment and literal square domain] For $\varphi\in D(\varepsilon)$, expand $\varepsilon_n^2=\sum_i\varepsilon(k_i)^2+\sum_{i\ne j}\varepsilon(k_i)\varepsilon(k_j)$ and integrate against $\prod_i\|\varphi(k_i)\|^2$. Tonelli gives $\|T_n\Phi_n\|^2=n\|\varepsilon\varphi\|^2+n(n-1)\bar\varepsilon^2$, finite by the stated domain and Cauchy-Schwarz. This is the spectral second moment and requires no $T_n^2\Phi_n$. If $\varphi\in D(\varepsilon^2)$, the inequality $(\sum_{i=1}^n\varepsilon(k_i))^4\le n^3\sum_i\varepsilon(k_i)^4$ gives $\|T_n^2\Phi_n\|^2\le n^4\|\varepsilon^2\varphi\|^2<\infty$, so $\Phi_n\in D(T_n^2)$; self-adjointness then gives $\langle T_n^2\Phi_n,\Phi_n\rangle=\|T_n\Phi_n\|^2$, exactly the original operator-square display. The vacuum has energy zero and all its moments vanish, handled separately when $n=0$. [F6, step 1.1, algebra] ∎
