citations.quote: Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H,K$ be complex Hilbert spaces with the pairing linear in the first argument ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]], [[def-hilbert-space]]). Write $H\odot K$ for the complex vector space of [[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]] applied to $R=\mathbb C$ and the $\mathbb C$-modules $H,K$: its underlying abelian group is the quotient $F/H_0$ of that definition, the class of $e_{(u,v)}$ is written $u\otimes v$, every element of $H\odot K$ is a finite sum of elementary tensors $u\otimes v$, and the defining relations make $(u,v)\mapsto u\otimes v$ $\mathbb C$-bilinear. Define, for finite sums, $$\Bigl\langle\sum_i u_i\otimes v_i,\ \sum_j u'_j\otimes v'_j\Bigr\rangle:=\sum_{i,j}\langle u_i,u'_j\rangle_H\,\langle v_i,v'_j\rangle_K .$$ Then: (a) *well-definedness and sesquilinearity*: the displayed value is independent of the representatives of its two arguments and defines a Hermitian sesquilinear form on $H\odot K$, linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second; (b) *positive definiteness and orthonormal coordinates*: $\langle z,z\rangle\ge0$ for every $z\in H\odot K$, with $\langle z,z\rangle=0$ exactly for $z=0$; more precisely, if $U_0\subseteq H$ and $V_0\subseteq K$ are finite-dimensional subspaces with orthonormal bases $e_1,\dots,e_p$ and $f_1,\dots,f_q$, then every $z$ in the span of the elementary tensors from $U_0\times V_0$ has a unique expansion $z=\sum_{a,b}c_{ab}\,e_a\otimes f_b$ and $\langle z,z\rangle=\sum_{a,b}|c_{ab}|^2$; in particular the assignment is an inner product on $H\odot K$; (c) *completion*: the norm completion $(\widehat{H\odot K},\kappa)$ of $H\odot K$ ([[def-completion-of-a-normed-space]]) exists and, with the unique inner product extending the given one, is a complex Hilbert space; $\kappa$ is a linear isometry with dense image, $\|\kappa(u\otimes v)\|=\|u\|\,\|v\|$, and any two completions of $H\odot K$ are identified by a unique surjective linear isometry fixing $H\odot K$ pointwise; (d) *product bases*: if $(e_a)_{a\in A}$ and $(f_b)_{b\in B}$ are orthonormal families in $H$ and $K$ whose closed linear spans are $H$ and $K$, then $(\kappa(e_a\otimes f_b))_{(a,b)\in A\times B}$ is an orthonormal family in $\widehat{H\odot K}$ whose closed linear span is $\widehat{H\odot K}$; if $A$ and $B$ are countable then $\widehat{H\odot K}$ is separable. The notation $H\widehat{\otimes}K:=\widehat{H\odot K}$ is used in the rest of this pair. No assertion is made about unbounded operators or algebraic sums of non-completed tensor products.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H,H',K,K'$ be complex Hilbert spaces and let $S\in\mathcal B(H,H')$, $T\in\mathcal B(K,K')$ be bounded linear operators ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). Write $H\widehat\otimes K$ for the completion of the algebraic tensor product constructed in [[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]], with inclusion $\kappa$. (a) There is a unique bounded linear operator $S\otimes T: H\widehat\otimes K\to H'\widehat\otimes K'$ with $(S\otimes T)\kappa(u\otimes v)=\kappa'(Su\otimes Tv)$ for all $u\in H$, $v\in K$, and it satisfies $\|S\otimes T\|\le\|S\|\,\|T\|$ ([[def-operator-norm]]). (b) For Hilbert spaces $H'',K''$ and bounded $S':H''\to H$, $T':K''\to K$, one has $(S\otimes T)(S'\otimes T')=(SS')\otimes(TT')$. In particular, for endomorphisms $S:H\to H$, $T:K\to K$, the endomorphisms $S\otimes I_K$ and $I_H\otimes T$ commute and their composite is $S\otimes T$. (c) The Hilbert adjoint ([[def-hilbert-space-adjoint]]) is $(S\otimes T)^*=S^*\otimes T^*$. (d) If $S,T$ are unitary, then so is $S\otimes T$. No extension of unbounded maps, and no algebraic manipulation of domains of unbounded operators, is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), let $a,b\ge1$ and identify $\mathbb R^{a+b}=\mathbb R^a\times\mathbb R^b$ with Lebesgue measure ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]); write $H_a=L^2(\mathbb R^a)$, $H_b=L^2(\mathbb R^b)$. Then there is a unique linear isometry $$\Theta:H_a\widehat\otimes H_b\longrightarrow L^2(\mathbb R^{a+b})$$ with $\Theta(f\otimes g)(x,y)=f(x)g(y)$ for all $f\in H_a$, $g\in H_b$ and a.e. $(x,y)$, and $\Theta$ is onto: it is a surjective linear isometry, hence unitary. Vector-valued or spin factors follow by finite component sums. No identification of non-Euclidean product measures is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space, $n\ge1$, and $H^{\otimes n}$ the $n$-fold completed tensor power ($H^{\otimes1}:=H$, $H^{\otimes(k+1)}:=H^{\otimes k}\widehat\otimes H$ as in [[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]]). For $v_1,\dots,v_n\in H$ write $v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n\in H^{\otimes n}$ for the iterated elementary tensor. (a) For every $\pi$ in the symmetric group $S_n$ ([[def-finite-symmetric-group-and-permutation-notation]]) there is a unique unitary $U_\pi\in\mathcal B(H^{\otimes n})$ with $$U_\pi(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)=v_{\pi^{-1}(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{\pi^{-1}(n)},$$ and $U_\pi U_\sigma=U_{\pi\sigma}$, $U_{\pi}^*=U_{\pi^{-1}}$. (b) The operators $$P_+:=\frac1{n!}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}U_\pi,\qquad P_-:=\frac1{n!}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)U_\pi$$ (with $\operatorname{sgn}$ the sign homomorphism, [[thm-sign-is-a-homomorphism]]) are orthogonal projections. (c) $U_\pi P_+=P_+U_\pi=P_+$ and $U_\pi P_-=P_-U_\pi=\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)P_-$ for every $\pi$; consequently the range of $P_+$ is the subspace of vectors fixed by every $U_\pi$, and the range of $P_-$ is the subspace of vectors transforming by $\operatorname{sgn}$. (d) If $v_1,\dots,v_n$ are not pairwise distinct in the sense that $v_i=v_j$ for some $i\ne j$, then $P_-(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)=0$; in particular, for $n\ge2$, $P_-(u\otimes u\otimes w_3\otimes\cdots\otimes w_n)=0$ for all $u,w_k\in H$. Selecting the symmetric or antisymmetric sector for a particle species is a physical postulate, not a theorem of this construction; no spin-statistics statement is proved here.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]), let $d\ge1$ and work on $H=L^2(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ ([[def-hilbert-space]]). (a) For a real measurable finite-valued function $a:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ define $M_af:=af$ on $D(M_a):=\{f\in H: af\in H\}$. Then $M_a$ is a densely defined self-adjoint operator on $H$ ([[def-adjoint-of-a-densely-defined-unbounded-operator]], [[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]]). (b) Let $c>0$, $b\in\mathbb R$, and let $\mathcal F_2$ be the unitary Plancherel transform with the convention $\widehat f(\xi)=\int f(x)e^{-2\pi ix\cdot\xi}dx$ on $L^1$ ([[def-fourier-transform-on-l-one-of-rn]], [[thm-plancherel]]). Define $$H_0:=\mathcal F_2^*\,M_{c|\xi|^2+b}\,\mathcal F_2,\qquad D(H_0):=\{f\in H:|\xi|^2\mathcal F_2f\in H\}.$$ Then $H_0$ is self-adjoint, $D(H_0)$ coincides with the Sobolev space $W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ as a set (with equivalent norms, [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], [[thm-fourier-characterisation-of-integer-order-hilbert-sobolev-spaces]]), $H_0\ge b$ in the quadratic-form sense, and for every Schwartz function $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$, $H_0f=-(c/4\pi^2)\Delta f+bf$. (c) If $V:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ is measurable with $\|V\|_\infty<\infty$ and $H:=H_0+M_V$ with domain $D(H_0)$, then $H$ is self-adjoint on $D(H_0)$, is bounded below, and the assignment $t\mapsto e^{itH}$ is a strongly continuous one-parameter unitary group whose generator is $-iH$: the limit $\lim_{t\to0}\frac1t(e^{itH}\psi-\psi)$ exists exactly for $\psi\in D(H)$ and equals $iH\psi$ ([[lem-self-adjoint-operator-generates-a-strongly-continuous-unitary-group]]). (d) *Scope*: the argument uses only boundedness and measurability of $V$; it proves nothing for $V\propto-1/|x|$, $V\propto|x|^2$ or the delta interaction, does not identify $H_0$ with any measured free-particle Hamiltonian, and asserts no physical interpretation.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$ be a $\sigma$-finite measure space with $\mu(X)>0$, let $m:X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable and finite $\mu$-almost everywhere, and on the complex Hilbert space $H=L^{2}(X,\mu;\mathbb C)$ ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]], [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]], [[def-hilbert-space]]) let $$D(M_{m})=\Bigl\{f\in H:\int_{X}|m|^{2}|f|^{2}\,d\mu<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad M_{m}f=mf .$$ Then: (a) $M_{m}$ is self-adjoint on $D(M_{m})$ ([[thm-nrqm-composites-real-multipliers-and-free-bounded-potential-operators]] clause (a)). (b) The assignment $E(B):=M_{\mathbf 1_{m^{-1}(B)}}$ on Borel sets $B\subseteq\mathbb R$ is a regular projection-valued measure on the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $\mathbb R$ ([[def-projection-valued-measure]]), and for a unit vector $\psi\in H$ $$\|E(B)\psi\|^{2}=\int_{m^{-1}(B)}|\psi|^{2}\,d\mu .$$ (c) The operator identity $\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda\,dE(\lambda)=M_{m}$ holds with domain $D(M_{m})$ ([[def-unbounded-integral-against-a-pvm]]); consequently $E$ is the spectral projection-valued measure of $M_{m}$ ([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]]). (d) $E(B)=0$ if and only if $\mu(m^{-1}(B))=0$, and the spectrum $\sigma(M_{m})$ equals the essential range of $m$: $$\sigma(M_{m})=\{\,t\in\mathbb R:\mu(m^{-1}(t-\varepsilon,t+\varepsilon))>0\ \text{for every}\ \varepsilon>0\,\}.$$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(X,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space, let $H$ be a nonzero complex Hilbert space, let $E$ be a projection valued measure on $(X,\Sigma)$, and let $f:X\to\mathbb C$ be bounded and $\Sigma$-measurable ([[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]). Then: 1. there is a unique operator $\Phi_E(f)\in\mathcal B(H)$ with $$\langle\Phi_E(f)x,y\rangle=\int f\,dE_{x,y}\qquad(x,y\in H),$$ and for every sequence $(s_n)$ of complex simple functions with $\|f-s_n\|_\infty\to0$ one has $\|\Phi_E(f)-\int s_n\,dE\|\to0$: the integral is obtained from uniform simple approximations and is independent of the approximating sequence; 2. $\|\Phi_E(f)\|\le\|f\|_\infty$, and for every $x\in H$ $$\langle\Phi_E(f)x,x\rangle=\int f\,dE_x,\qquad \|\Phi_E(f)x\|^2=\int|f|^2\,dE_x ;$$ 3. the exact norm is the **$E$-essential supremum** $$\|f\|_{E,\infty}:=\sup\bigl\{\|f\|_{\infty,E_x}:\ x\in H,\ \|x\|=1\bigr\}, \qquad \|\Phi_E(f)\|=\|f\|_{E,\infty},$$ where $\|f\|_{\infty,E_x}$ denotes the essential supremum of the real measurable function $|f|$ with respect to the finite measure $E_x$ ([[def-essential-supremum-with-respect-to-a-measure]]).

Assume Countable Choice. Let $E$ be a projection valued measure on the measurable space $(X,\Sigma)$ acting on the complex Hilbert space $H$ ([[def-projection-valued-measure]]), and let $f:X\to\mathbb C$ be $\Sigma$-measurable. Put $$D(f(E)):=\Bigl\{x\in H:\int_X|f|^2\,dE_x<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad E_x(B)=\langle E(B)x,x\rangle,$$ where the scalar measures $E_x$ are those of [[lem-scalar-and-complex-measures-from-a-pvm]], and for $x\in D(f(E))$ set $$f(E)x:=\lim_{n\to\infty}\Phi_E\bigl(f\,\mathbf 1_{\{|f|\le n\}}\bigr)x,$$ For $H\ne\{0\}$, the bounded integrals $\Phi_E$ are those of [[thm-bounded-borel-pvm-integral]], and the limit is taken in the norm of $H$. For $H=\{0\}$, define $\Phi_E(g)$ to be the unique operator on $H$ for every bounded measurable $g$. Then $E_0$ is the zero measure, $D(f(E))=H$, and $f(E)0=0$. Thus this case is defined directly without applying a theorem requiring a nonzero space. **Well-definedness.** $D(f(E))$ is a linear subspace: the estimate $E_{x+y}\le2E_x+2E_y$ for scalar measures and $E_{\alpha x}=|\alpha|^2E_x$ follow from $\|E(B)(x+y)\|^2\le2\|E(B)x\|^2+2\|E(B)y\|^2$ and $\|E(B)\alpha x\|^2=|\alpha|^2\|E(B)x\|^2$. Writing $f_n:=f\mathbf 1_{\{|f|\le n\}}$ the sets $\{|f|\le n\}$ are measurable, so $f_n$ is bounded and measurable. For $m,n\ge N$, $$|f_n-f_m|^2\le |f|^2\mathbf1_{\{|f|>N\}}.$$ The integral of the right side against $E_x$ tends to zero by [[thm-dominated-convergence]], with the integrable majorant $|f|^2$ and pointwise limit zero since $f$ is finite-valued. Linearity of the bounded calculus ([[thm-pvm-integral-is-a-star-homomorphism]]) and its quadratic identity give $$\|\Phi_E(f_n)x-\Phi_E(f_m)x\|^2=\int|f_n-f_m|^2\,dE_x.$$ These clauses hold directly on the zero space as well. Hence the truncation vectors are Cauchy and converge uniquely by Hilbert-space completeness ([[def-hilbert-space]]). The limit is linear in $x$ because every truncation operator is linear and addition and scalar multiplication are norm-continuous. Countable Choice is inherited from the bounded PVM suppliers; no further choice is needed to take these specified limits. Finally, if two $\Sigma$-measurable functions $f,g$ agree outside a measurable set $N$ with $E(N)=0$, then $E_x(N)=\|E(N)x\|^2=0$ for every $x$. Thus the integrals of $|f|^2$ and $|g|^2$ agree, so their domains agree. At every truncation level their bounded truncations agree outside $N$; the quadratic identity applied to the difference gives equal truncation vectors for every $x$. Taking limits gives $f(E)x=g(E)x$ on their common domain.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $E$ be a projection valued measure on $(X,\Sigma)$ on the complex Hilbert space $H$ and let $f:X\to\mathbb C$ be $\Sigma$-measurable. Then the operator $f(E)$ of [[def-unbounded-integral-against-a-pvm]] is densely defined and closed, and it is normal, in the sense $D(f(E))=D(f(E)^*)$ and equal norms for the operator and its adjoint; in particular $D(f(E))=D(\overline f(E))$ and $\|f(E)x\|=\|\overline f(E)x\|$ for all such $x$. Moreover $$\|f(E)x\|^2=\int|f|^2\,dE_x,\qquad \langle x,f(E)x\rangle=\int\overline f\,dE_x\qquad(x\in D(f(E))),$$ and $(f(E))^*=\overline f(E)$; in particular $f(E)$ is self-adjoint whenever $f$ takes real values. Finally, if $(g_n)$ are bounded $\Sigma$-measurable functions with $|g_n|\le C|f|$ pointwise and $g_n\to f$ pointwise, then $g_n(E)x\to f(E)x$ for every $x\in D(f(E))$.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be an arbitrary complex Hilbert space, with inner product linear in the first variable, and let $A=A^*$ be a densely defined self-adjoint operator on $H$. There is no separability or supplied-basis hypothesis on $H$. There is a unique regular projection-valued Borel measure $E_A$ on $\mathbb R$ representing $A$, with $E_A(\mathbb R)=I$, strong countable additivity and $$D(A)=\{x:\int\lambda^2d\mu_x(\lambda)<\infty\},\qquad \|Ax\|^2=\int\lambda^2d\mu_x,\qquad \mu_x(B)=\langle E_A(B)x,x\rangle.$$ Regularity means compact inner and open outer approximation of each finite scalar measure $\mu_x$. For bounded Borel $b$, its calculus satisfies $\|b(A)\|\le\sup|b|$, $(bc)(A)=b(A)c(A)$ and $\overline b(A)=b(A)^*$. For finite-valued, possibly unbounded complex Borel $b$, there is a closed densely defined operator $b(A)$ on exactly $\{x:\int|b|^2d\mu_x<\infty\}$, with norm given by that integral and convergence of the bounded cutoffs on its domain. The PVM is concentrated on $\sigma(A)$, and a real $\lambda$ belongs to $\sigma(A)$ exactly when every neighborhood of $\lambda$ has nonzero spectral projection. For $z\notin\sigma(A)$, the bounded resolvent is the multiplier $(\lambda-z)^{-1}$, maps into exactly $D(A)$, and has norm at most $\operatorname{dist}(z,\sigma(A))^{-1}$ (with the zero-space convention $1/\infty=0$). The operators $U_A(t)=e^{itA}$ form a strongly continuous unitary group on all of $H$, with the exact derivative criterion $$\lim_{t\to0}\frac{U_A(t)x-x}{t}\text{ exists in }H\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x\in D(A),\qquad \left.\frac{d}{dt}U_A(t)x\right|_{t=0}=iAx.$$ They preserve $D(A)$ and its graph norm and commute with $A$ on that domain. The group with this exact generator is unique. PVMs, Borel calculus and groups transport under unitary intertwiners, and an isometry intertwining the groups for all real times has a reducing closed range and intertwines the PVMs. The construction uses countably generated subspaces attached to each finite tuple of vectors and their uniquely determined compatible calculus; it does not choose an arbitrary global cyclic decomposition or an orthonormal basis of $H$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space with inner product linear in the first argument ([[def-hilbert-space]], [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). Let $H^{\otimes 0}:=\mathbb C$, $H^{\otimes 1}:=H$ and $H^{\otimes(n+1)}:=H^{\otimes n}\widehat\otimes H$ be the completed tensor powers with elementary tensors $u_1\otimes\cdots\otimes u_n$ ([[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]]); for $n\ge 1$ let $P_+^{(n)}\in\mathcal B(H^{\otimes n})$ be the symmetric projection of [[lem-nrqm-composites-permutation-sector-projections]] and set $P_+^{(0)}:=\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb C}$. Write $\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$ for its range and define $$F(H):=\Bigl\{\psi=(\psi_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}:\ \psi_n\in\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}\ \text{for all }n,\ \sum_{n\in\mathbb N}\|\psi_n\|^2<\infty\Bigr\}.$$ Then: (a) for $\psi,\varphi\in F(H)$ the scalar series $\sum_{n\in\mathbb N}\langle\psi_n,\varphi_n\rangle$ converges absolutely and defines a sesquilinear form, linear in the first argument, with respect to which $F(H)$ is a complex vector space with inner product $\langle\psi,\varphi\rangle:=\sum_{n\in\mathbb N}\langle\psi_n,\varphi_n\rangle$ ([[cor-cauchy-schwarz-inequality-for-l-two]], [[def-series-and-absolute-convergence-in-a-normed-space]]); (b) $(F(H),\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle)$ is a Hilbert space, i.e. the induced norm is complete ([[def-hilbert-space]]); (c) the vacuum vector $\Omega:=(1,0,0,\dots)$ satisfies $\|\Omega\|=1$, and the finite-particle space $F_0:=\{\psi\in F(H):\psi_n=0\ \text{for all but finitely many }n\}$ is a dense linear subspace of $F(H)$ ([[def-dense-top]]); (d) for every $n$ the map $\iota_n:\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}\to F(H)$, $\iota_n(u):=(0,\dots,0,u,0,\dots)$ (entry in coordinate $n$) is a linear isometry of $\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$ onto the closed subspace of vectors supported in coordinate $n$; (e) if $H$ admits a countable complete orthonormal family $(e_i)_{i\in I}$, $I$ at most countable ([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]), then $F(H)$ is separable ([[def-separable-space]]); (f) *direct sums of self-adjoint operators*: if for every $n\ge 1$ a self-adjoint operator $T_n$ on the Hilbert space $\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$ with domain $D(T_n)\subseteq\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$ is given ([[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]], [[def-unbounded-linear-operator-domain-and-graph]]), and $$D(T):=\Bigl\{\psi\in F(H):\ \psi_n\in D(T_n)\ \text{for all }n,\ \sum_{n\in\mathbb N}\|T_n\psi_n\|^2<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad (T\psi)_n:=T_n\psi_n,$$ then $T$ is self-adjoint and $D(T)$ is dense; if in addition every $T_n$ is bounded with $\sup_{n}\|T_n\|<\infty$, then $T$ is bounded with $\|T\|=\sup_n\|T_n\|$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). No physical interpretation of $F(H)$, of the tensor powers or of the direct-sum operators is asserted.

derivations.claim: [Explicit transverse tensor embedding] The measurable matrices $\Pi(k)$ are orthogonal projections with norm at most one. Hence $M_\Pi$ is a bounded orthogonal projection on $G$, with range exactly $\mathfrak h$, because $\Pi(k)f(k)=f(k)$ is equivalent to $k\cdot f(k)=0$ off the null point $0$. In particular $\mathfrak h$ is closed and Hilbert. The inclusion $\mathfrak h\to G$ induces an isometric inclusion of every finite tensor power: its elementary-tensor inner products agree by [F1], and density extends that isometry to the completion. Its closed range is the range of $(M_\Pi)^{\otimes n}$, since the latter projection maps the dense elementary span onto elementary transverse tensors. Iterating [F1] with dimensions $3,3(n-1)$ and finite components gives a unitary $\Theta_n:G^{\otimes n}\to L_n$ with the stated product formula. Under it $(M_\Pi)^{\otimes n}$ becomes multiplication by $Q_n(k)=\Pi(k_1)\otimes\cdots\otimes\Pi(k_n)$: both bounded maps agree on all elementary tensors, hence on their dense span. No undocumented product-measure or tensor-subspace identification is used. [given, F1, construct, algebra]

[Symmetry includes polarization permutations] Define the unitary $\tau_\pi$ on $(\mathbb C^3)^{\otimes n}$ by the same tensor-factor permutation as in [F2]. The conjugated ambient permutation is $(C_\pi u)(k_1,\ldots,k_n)=\tau_\pi u(k_{\pi(1)},\ldots,k_{\pi(n)})$: substitution into the elementary product formula verifies this identity, and the bounded maps agree everywhere by density. Its average $S_n=(n!)^{-1}\sum_\pi C_\pi$ is the orthogonal symmetry projection. The tensor projection $(M_\Pi)^{\otimes n}$ commutes with every ambient permutation, as is verified on elementary tensors, so $M_{Q_n}$ commutes with $S_n$. Their product $R_n=M_{Q_n}S_n$ is an orthogonal projection, whose range is exactly the image of the symmetric transverse tensor sector. Thus $K_n=\operatorname{ran}R_n$ and $I_n=\Theta_n$ restricted to that sector is an isometry onto $K_n$. Every bounded scalar multiplier $b(p_{j,n})$ commutes with $M_{Q_n}$ pointwise and with $C_\pi$, since $p_{j,n}$ is invariant under permutations; therefore it commutes with $R_n$ and preserves $K_n$. [step 1.1, F1, F2, algebra]

[Sector PVM and regularity] The scalar function $p=p_{j,n}$ is real, measurable and finite on $\mathbb R^{3n}$. By [F3], multiplication by $\mathbf1_{p^{-1}(B)}$ is its spectral projection in each scalar component of $L_n$; the finite component sum is a regular PVM there. It commutes with $R_n$ by step 2.1. Its restriction to $K_n$, transported by $I_n$, is therefore an orthogonal projection for every $B$, with total projection $I$, product law and strong countable additivity inherited from the ambient PVM. Its scalar measure at $u$ is exactly $\int_{p^{-1}(B)}\|I_nu\|^2$, the sum of its finite component measures, so it is regular and is the push-forward of $\|I_nu\|^2d^{3n}k$. This defines the sector PVM $E_{j,n}$. For $n=0$, the indicated atom at zero is a regular PVM on $\mathbb C$. [step 2.1, F3, algebra]

[Exact signed sector domain and self-adjointness] For the PVM of step 3.1, push-forward integration gives $\int t^2\,dE_{j,n,u}(t)=\int |p(k)|^2\|I_nu(k)\|^2\,d^{3n}k$: it holds first for indicators and simple nonnegative functions and then for increasing nonnegative simple approximations. By [F4], $\int t\,dE_{j,n}(t)$ is densely defined and self-adjoint on exactly the displayed multiplier domain. For bounded Borel $b$, indicator/simple-function approximation and the norm estimate of [F4] show that $b(E_{j,n})$ is the restriction of multiplication by $b(p)$, transported by $I_n$. In particular the defining truncations for the identity function act as $p\mathbf1_{|p|\le L}I_nu$. If $pI_nu\in L_n$, these converge to $pI_nu$ in norm, because the integrable squared tail $\int_{|p|>L}|p|^2\|I_nu\|^2$ tends to zero. Every truncation lies in the closed $K_n$, so its limit lies there also. Thus the PVM integral is exactly $P_{j,n}$ with the stated action and domain. Spectral uniqueness [F4] identifies $E_{j,n}$ as its spectral PVM; $P_{j,0}=0$ is the corresponding vacuum operator. The sign of $p$ played no role in this squared-integrability argument. [step 2.1, step 3.1, F4, algebra]

[Total operator and its maximal domain] By step 4.1 every sector operator is self-adjoint. Applying [F5] gives self-adjointness and density of their direct sum on the exact domain in (b), with $\|P_{j,n}\psi_n\|^2=\int|p_{j,n}|^2\|I_n\psi_n\|^2$ for $n\ge1$ and zero for $n=0$. This also proves the equivalent integral-domain description. More explicitly, density follows by first truncating the number of sectors and then applying the bounded $|p_{j,n}|\le L$ cutoffs in the remaining finitely many sectors. No requirement is imposed on the separate coordinate multipliers; only the summed $p_{j,n}$ enters the domain. [step 4.1, F5, algebra]

[The Fock PVM and push-forward sum] For each Borel $B$, $E_j(B)=\bigoplus_nE_{j,n}(B)$ is a bounded orthogonal projection of norm at most one, with the product law and total projection $I$. Strong countable additivity follows sectorwise and then on the full sum: first retain finitely many sectors, where convergence is already known, and bound the omitted squared tail by $\sum_{n>N}\|\psi_n\|^2$, which tends to zero uniformly in the partial union. Its scalar measure is the displayed sum in (b), with total mass $\|\psi\|^2$. It is regular: for any fixed Borel set and error $\varepsilon>0$, choose finitely many sector measures leaving total tail mass below $\varepsilon/2$; approximate that set from inside by a compact set for each of the finitely many regular measures and take their finite union, or from outside by open sets and take their finite intersection, allocating the remaining error among those measures. This proves compact inner and open outer approximation for the full scalar measure. Finally nonnegative integration of the scalar sum gives $\int t^2\,dE_{j,\psi}=\sum_n\|P_{j,n}\psi_n\|^2$, allowing infinity; the identity follows from indicators, simple functions and their increasing approximations. Bounded PVM integrals act sectorwise, and the identity-function truncations converge on this exact domain to $(P_{j,n}\psi_n)_n$, with squared error equal to the decreasing integrable spectral tail. Hence $\int t\,dE_j(t)=P_j$ on precisely $D(P_j)$. Regular spectral uniqueness [F4] makes $E_j$ its spectral PVM. [step 3.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, F4, F5, algebra]

[Vacuum, one-particle restriction and scope] The vacuum has only its zeroth component, where $P_{j,0}=0$, so it belongs to $D(P_j)$ and $P_j\Omega=0$. For $n=1$, $\Theta_1=I_G$ and the symmetric projection is the identity, so the sector construction gives exactly the maximal restricted multiplier $f\mapsto\hbar k_jf$ on $\mathfrak h$. Steps 1.1–6.1 establish all tensor embeddings, sector domains, self-adjointness and PVM formulas without importing any physical radiation postulate. CC and AC are the declared hypotheses of the actual mathematical suppliers; no positivity, dispersion relation, commutation between distinct unbounded observables or physical law was used. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, step 6.1, algebra] ∎
